overview: Mi'kma'ki is the homeland of the Mi'kmaq, not a centralized country founded in 1492. The atlas id runs 1492 to 1783; Mi'kmaq people, language, law, and relationships are much older and continue. Its changing polygons are imported artwork: seven snapshots use five distinct geometry regimes, and the 1600 map even splits one id into two features. Mi'kmaw teaching describes seven districts shaped by watersheds and governance, with decisions moving through families, communities, Saqmaq, and the Sante' Mawio'mi. No one Saqmaw represented every community. People drew food and materials from coasts, rivers, forests, and islands; built homes and watercraft; raised children through family and oral learning; traded and negotiated widely; and adapted without surrendering identity. French and British settlement, missions, epidemics, wars, and resource pressure caused severe disruption. Peace and Friendship Treaties from 1725 through 1779 did not cede the homeland. Written-language sample: none reproduced here. A missionary-linked logographic system is documented from 1677, but the reviewed sources do not provide one securely attributable exact-period glyph sequence paired with a complete original Mi'kmaw reading and contemporary translation that can be reproduced responsibly.

periods.title: 1492 to 1534: an old homeland, not a new state
periods.summary: The imported feature begins in 1492, but no Mi'kmaw founding event matches that seam. Communities already knew coasts, rivers, portages, food places, kin routes, and seasonal work. Archaeology and Mi'kmaw knowledge support long continuity; the hard polygon and inherited state label do not.

periods.title: 1534 to 1604: contact and exchange widen
periods.summary: Cartier entered Chaleur Bay in 1534, planted a French claim, and met Indigenous people in a busy maritime region. European fisheries and trade expanded afterward. Evidence for Mi'kmaw presence also reaches Newfoundland, but dates, routes, and identities require care rather than a single sudden contact story.

periods.title: 1604 to 1632: Port-Royal, alliance, and mission
periods.summary: French settlers entered Mi'kma'ki and depended on Mi'kmaw knowledge and welcome. Membertou helped shape alliance and exchange at Port-Royal; Mi'kmaq safeguarded the Habitation from 1607 to 1610. His family's 1610 baptism records mission pressure and diplomacy, not wholesale cultural replacement.

periods.title: 1632 to 1675: renewed colonization and negotiated change
periods.summary: French colonial presence revived in Acadia after 1632, while trade goods, missionaries, and merchants became more persistent. Mi'kmaq selected and reworked new materials while maintaining food systems, mobility, authority, and law. Seventeenth-century synthesis supports change without proving instant dependence or universal conversion.

periods.title: 1675 to 1713: writing, war, and resilient authority
periods.summary: A missionary-linked Mi'kmaw logographic system is documented from 1677, chiefly for Catholic texts and memorization. European imperial wars brought danger, while Mi'kmaw leaders pursued their own alliances and territorial aims. Utrecht in 1713 transferred French claims to Britain without Mi'kmaw land cession or consent.

periods.title: 1713 to 1726: resistance leads to treaty
periods.summary: British fishing and settlement pressure increased after Utrecht. Mi'kmaw resistance included seizing vessels and fighting, while communities and leaders negotiated from different positions. A 1725 Boston agreement was ratified at Annapolis Royal in 1726 by Mi'kmaw and neighboring leaders, beginning a linked treaty sequence.

periods.title: 1726 to 1761: treaties amid forts and imperial war
periods.summary: Treaty relationships were renewed while Mi'kmaq also maintained alliance with France. Halifax, forts, settler arrivals, warfare, and the Acadian deportation transformed the region. The 1752 agreement did not bind every community; nine Mi'kmaw communities made peace in 1760 and 1761 after major French defeats.

periods.title: 1761 to 1783: living treaties outlast the map
periods.summary: Peace and Friendship Treaties continued through 1779 on unceded lands. Mi'kmaw delegates signed the unratified 1776 Treaty of Watertown during the American Revolution, while different communities made their own decisions. The exact feature vanishes at 1783, but Mi'kma'ki, Mi'kmaq communities, treaty rights, and governance continue.

items.text: The exact index record is mi-kma-ki, labeled Mi'kma'ki and dated approximately 1492 to 1783. Coverage finds seven border snapshots and no finished card. Those fields describe an imported map layer; they do not date the beginning of Mi'kmaq people, homeland, governance, or law.

Mi'kma'ki names the homeland of the Mi'kmaq. Mi'kmaw teaching connects people, land, animals, language, stories, and law across seven traditional districts. Calling this card a culture and homeland corrects the inherited state label without reducing living political authority to folklore or geography alone.

Across seven present snapshots, the exact id uses eight features and five geometry regimes. It begins as five components, narrows to two, splits into separate mainland and Cape Breton polygons in 1600, then adds a Newfoundland component by 1650. These are cartographic edits, not dated annexations.

The hard-edged polygons overlap other indexed peoples and colonial features, while familiar places cross in and out as shapes change. Homeland, harvesting, kinship, travel, and treaty relationships cannot be read as exclusive pixel ownership. The geometry must be preserved for the map while its historical limits remain visible.

Mi'kma'ki and the later Wabanaki Confederacy are related histories, not aliases. Mi'kmaq participated in wider alliances, yet Mi'kmaw communities, districts, and Saqmaq retained authority. No one leader spoke automatically for all others, so this card has no appliesTo link to a single confederate state.

Mi'kmaw teaching describes seven districts whose geography follows watersheds and other landforms. Districts supported governance and responsibility rather than surveyed international frontiers. Rivers, bays, coasts, islands, and portages connected communities, food places, and councils, so water routes belong at the center of this regional history.

At Kejimkujik, more than sixty sites record camps, fish weirs, portages, trails, burials, and long use between inland waters and the coast. The area supported part-year residence, freshwater foods, and travel. One protected landscape illustrates skilled movement without supplying a universal calendar for all Mi'kma'ki.

Archaeological places need stewardship as well as excavation. Mi'kmawey Debert explains that protection, community authority, and changing interpretation shape what can be learned. A site is not merely a box of artifacts, and one protected place should never become a settlement model imposed on every district.

Debert archaeology reaches far earlier than this card and shows sophisticated knowledge, hearths, tools, travel, care, and wide connections. It establishes deep human history in Mi'kma'ki, not a direct family tree for every later community. The site also teaches how evidence leaves some questions unanswered.

The atlas adds a Newfoundland component after 1650, but academic research treats Mi'kmaw presence there as a historical question with changing evidence. A newly painted component cannot settle migration dates, sovereignty, ancestry, or the identities of every occupant. Map coverage and historical argument remain separate.

Cartier's 1534 voyage reached Chaleur Bay and made a French claim in a region already inhabited and traveled. His expedition is an outsider source with its own aims. It dates one encounter horizon, but it does not mark European discovery of an empty land or Mi'kmaq consent to France.

Before permanent French settlement, seasonal European fisheries and exchange brought metal, cloth, and other goods into Atlantic networks. Mi'kmaq participants chose what to trade, keep, alter, or reject. Material change therefore records Indigenous decisions as well as colonial pressure, not a one-way march from stone to metal.

At Port-Royal, French settlers relied on Mi'kmaw welcome, knowledge, food, and alliance. Parks Canada records that the Mi'kmaq cared for the Habitation between the French departure in 1607 and return in 1610. This reverses stories that cast newcomers as self-sufficient founders of Mi'kma'ki.

Membertou was a regional Mi'kmaw leader, diplomat, and alliance builder at Port-Royal. His family's 1610 Catholic baptism occurred within negotiation and colonial mission activity. It should not be presented as the conversion of all Mi'kmaq, the surrender of Mi'kma'ki, or the start of one centralized government.

Missionaries and merchants depended on translation, hosts, guides, kin connections, and negotiated access. Their writings are indispensable but partial, often centering European goals. Archaeology can show adopted objects and changing practices, while neither source type reveals every conversation, refusal, private belief, or household strategy.

Mi'kmaq food systems joined coastal fish and shellfish, freshwater fish, birds, mammals, and useful plants in place-specific rounds. Kejimkujik evidence links inland residence with later coastal gathering. Availability varied by district, season, weather, and colonial disruption, so no single menu or monthly schedule fits every household.

Ethnohistorical and museum work describes bark-covered homes, hide clothing, sinew sewing, bone tools, pottery, cooking, hunting, fishing, and gathering. Much was recorded after contact, sometimes by observers with limited understanding. These accounts clarify technologies when cross-checked, but they are not a camera pointed at 1492.

Birchbark canoes, paddles, fish weirs, containers, cordage, shelters, and tailored clothing required detailed knowledge of trees, roots, hides, bone, stone, water, and weather. Calling these materials natural does not make the engineering automatic. Skilled makers planned, tested, repaired, taught, and adapted designs for different tasks.

At Malagomish, analyzed artifacts date roughly 250 to 1450 CE and test samples about 1600 to 380 calibrated years before present, so most evidence predates this card. The study chiefly supports environmental reconstruction and preservation limits, not exact 1492 to 1783 household diet, settlement, or sanitation rules.

A smoke opening helped a bark-covered home manage an indoor fire, though wind, coverings, maintenance, and fire size also mattered. It was practical ventilation, not proof that every dwelling had the same plan. Smoke, predictably, did not read the atlas border before choosing which way to drift.

Family sits at the heart of Mi'kmaw decision-making. Communities often remain clusters of extended kin, and important questions can begin with family-based Mi'kmawey before reaching community leadership. This supports strong relational government without fixing one household size, marriage rule, or residence pattern across three centuries.

Tpi'tnewey describes generous sharing of food, childcare, land use, and resources without demanding immediate repayment. Mi'kmaw teaching presents sharing as responsibility and blessing, not simple barter. The principle helps explain social security and prestige while avoiding a fantasy that scarcity, disagreement, or unequal colonial pressures never existed.

Saqmaq carried community responsibilities, while the Sante' Mawio'mi brought leaders from seven districts together on wider concerns. No Saqmaw automatically represented another community. Eighteenth-century treaties therefore required multiple decisions and signatures, a structure incompatible with treating the atlas polygon as one monarch's centralized jurisdiction.

Consensus aimed to work through disagreement rather than count a bare majority. Family, community, and district relationships all mattered, and compromise could take time. Historical accounts do not preserve every participant's voice, especially women's work and counsel, so silence in a colonial document must not become evidence of absence.

Mi'kmaw power appeared in knowledge, relationships, food access, diplomacy, sea travel, alliance, armed resistance, and the ability to make or refuse agreements. A society can exercise substantial power without palaces, tax rolls, or straight borders. Colonial records often noticed warfare more readily than everyday governance.

Children learned through family and community relationships, oral histories, observation, practice, correction, and increasing responsibility. Adults shared childcare, while elders carried valued experience. No surviving timetable lists a standard Mi'kma'ki school day for 1492, so learning is described through relationships rather than invented classrooms or grade levels.

Stories and memory carry law, place knowledge, values, history, and practical guidance through the Mi'kmaw language. Oral does not mean unreliable or unstructured. Treaty rights themselves require courts and historians to take Mi'kmaw oral knowledge seriously, while a written colonial archive remains selective and interested.

Young people learned values, stories, observation, sharing, relationships, and respectful behavior by joining family and community life. Exact ages, tasks, and divisions of labor are poorly documented for much of this period. The card therefore describes relational learning without inventing a fixed syllabus for every girl or boy.

Mi'kmaw teaching explains qalipu, the source of English caribou, through the animal's action of shoveling snow for food. It is a memorable language lesson, not a claim that every old word has one simple English equivalent. A good noun, apparently, may arrive carrying its own tiny snow shovel.

Debert interpretation allows that knowledgeable people cared, solved problems, disagreed, and found humor in daily life, while admitting how much remains unknown. No datable joke survives for this card. Humor can be recognized as human continuity without inventing a punchline or turning sacred beings into entertainment.

Food knowledge, shelter, clothing, fire, cooperation, and seasonal planning plausibly supported health before any named treatment began. That is a careful inference from lifeways, not a surviving clinical manual. Care can include nourishment, warmth, rest, and relationships without inventing one standardized Mi'kmaw clinic or diagnosis.

Later records document Mi'kmaw knowledge of medicinal plants and healing practices. They can demonstrate continuity and expertise, but a remedy written down in the nineteenth or twentieth century is not automatically a prescription from 1492. This card does not supply dosages, guaranteed effects, or a timeless universal plant list.

Sweating, bathing, smoke, plant preparations, diet, and skilled caregiving appear in historical accounts with different dates and reliability. Some practices combined physical, social, and spiritual dimensions that European observers misunderstood. They should be attributed carefully instead of sorted into modern boxes labeled medicine, religion, or hygiene.

European-introduced infections contributed to severe Indigenous loss, but epidemic dates, routes, mortality, and diagnoses are often uncertain. Scholars warn against repeating dramatic numbers without evidence or treating disease as an automatic event at first contact. Warfare, displacement, hunger, and colonial disruption also shaped vulnerability and survival.

Individual experiences of childbirth, disability, injury, aging, grief, and recovery rarely survive in exact-period sources. Family and community care are historically important, yet the record cannot supply identical roles or outcomes. Naming those silences respects people better than filling them with confident medical stories colonial observers never recorded.

Rivers, lakes, and coastal places supported travel, fishing, food work, and camp locations; people also needed fresh water for drinking and cooking. Sources and conditions varied by season and place. The evidence does not establish one purification method, daily allowance, well design, or piped system across Mi'kma'ki.

Fish weirs organized food capture in moving water, while canoe routes and portages linked inland and coastal systems. These works show planning and accumulated environmental knowledge. They do not prove that every community built the same structure or controlled water through a centralized public-works office.

Malagomish preserves shells, faunal remains, artifacts, charcoal, and layered deposits, but most dated evidence falls before this card begins. It offers deep background on preservation and repeated activity, not direct proof of 1492 to 1783 refuse routines. Reuse, burning, scattering, burial, and organic decay also leave unequal traces.

Indoor fires required fuel, placement, ventilation, and maintenance; outdoor camps created ash and food debris that people managed in ways archaeology only partly captures. Smoke openings and hearths show practical planning. They cannot reveal sweeping frequency, handwashing rules, or one shared standard of household cleanliness.

No reviewed source securely identifies a Mi'kmaw toilet, latrine design, sewer, or fecal-waste routine for 1492 to 1783. Temporary facilities and organic materials may leave little trace. Limited evidence does not mean people lacked privacy, designated places, or hygiene knowledge; it means the card should not invent them.

The 1725 Boston agreement was ratified by Mi'kmaw, Wolastoqey, and Peskotomuhkati leaders at Annapolis Royal in 1726. Later agreements renewed a linked Peace and Friendship relationship. Multiple ratifications reflect community authority; the familiar single-year label can hide years of separate decisions and signatories.

Mi'kmaw-French alliance grew from trade, kinship, religion, diplomacy, and shared resistance to British expansion. Annual renewal ceremonies included speeches, gifts, feasting, and military commitments. The alliance joined sovereign peoples with overlapping aims; it did not turn Mi'kmaq into French subjects or erase internal community choices.

The 1752 treaty involved Shubenacadie leader Jean-Baptiste Cope, while other leaders did not all sign. Forts, Halifax settlement, warfare, and the Acadian deportation intensified pressure. Treating one signature as surrender by every Mi'kmaw community would contradict the political structure and the surviving treaty sequence.

Nine Mi'kmaw communities made or renewed peace with Britain in 1760 and 1761 after French military defeats. These agreements protected continuing hunting, fishing, and trade relationships rather than ceding Mi'kma'ki. Modern treaty maps were corrected to include Quebec-based First Nations whose histories earlier mapping had omitted.

Mi'kmaw and Wolastoqey delegates signed an unratified Treaty of Watertown with Massachusetts in 1776 during the American Revolution; other treaty renewals continued through 1779. The record shows active diplomacy near the atlas endpoint. It does not make every district a single party or reduce treaties to colonial gifts.

sections.title: Art, writing, colonial disruption, and continuity

items.text: Kejimkujik's petroglyphs belong to a long Mi'kmaw cultural landscape, and Parks Canada dates the documented images mainly to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. A carved person, canoe, animal, or sign can communicate art and observation without becoming an alphabetic sentence that historians may freely translate.

A missionary-linked logographic system is documented from 1677 and was used especially to learn and recite Catholic texts. Mi'kmaq users copied and preserved signs, but surviving manuscripts and later descriptions have complex authorship. This history belongs inside the card without being mislabeled as a timeless pan-Mi'kmaw alphabet.

Written-language sample: none reproduced. The reviewed collection preserves a historical prayer-book tradition, yet it does not furnish a securely attributable exact-period glyph sequence paired with a complete original Mi'kmaw reading and contemporary translation that can be reproduced responsibly. Modern orthographies are valuable, but they are not substituted backward.

After the eighteenth century, governments increasingly ignored treaty responsibilities and attacked land, leadership, culture, women, children, and family systems. That later treaty-denial period explains profound disruption without turning 1783 into a disappearance. Colonial pressure changed life, while Mi'kmaq communities continued to govern, teach, remember, and adapt.

The atlas feature ends at 1783, yet Peace and Friendship Treaties, Mi'kmaw communities, the Sante' Mawio'mi, language, family networks, art, scholarship, and responsibilities to Mi'kma'ki continue. Archival and treaty education work now joins Mi'kmaw authority in correcting older records rather than treating people as a finished chapter.

ending.text: At 1783 the exact mi-kma-ki feature disappears from the atlas, but no reviewed source supports a matching end of Mi'kma'ki, the Mi'kmaq, or their political authority. Peace and Friendship Treaties continued through 1779 and remain living agreements on unceded lands. Afterward, settlement, resource loss, treaty denial, discriminatory law, and assimilation campaigns inflicted deep harm. Mi'kmaq families, communities, Saqmaq, the Sante' Mawio'mi, language, knowledge, art, treaty rights, and responsibilities to the homeland nevertheless continue. The endpoint is a software seam and colonial-era map transition, not conquest completed or a people vanished.
